statement: Each names a sinking, sorrowful turn of mind. cite.original: “Ekāyano ayaṁ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṁ visuddhiyā, sokaparidevānaṁ samatikkamāya, dukkhadomanassānaṁ atthaṅgamāya, ñāyassa adhigamāya, nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṁ cattāro satipaṭṭhānā.

cite.paraphrase: Contemplation of mind (citta). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating mind in mind. duḥkham ādhyātmikam ādhibhautikam ādhidaivikaṃ ca /
yenābhihatāḥ prāṇinas tadapaghātāya prayatante tad duḥkham /

cite.paraphrase: Pain (duḥkha) is of three kinds: relating to oneself (ādhyātmika), to other beings (ādhibhautika), and to the divine (ādhidaivika); it is that by which beings are struck and strive to strike it down. Dejection (daurmanasya) is a disturbance (kṣobha) of the mind through the frustration of a wish. Trembling of the limbs (aṅgamejayatva) is that which shakes the limbs. Inhalation (śvāsa) is when the vital breath (prāṇa) takes in outer air; exhalation (praśvāsa) is when it expels air from the belly. statement: Your words “i want to go straight back to it” fit only loosely what the Jain texts call Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling). Meditation (dhyāna) is of four kinds: sorrowful (ārta), cruel (raudra), virtuous (dharmya) and pure (śukla) (TS 9.28); the last two are causes of liberation (TS 9.29).

cite.title: Tattvārthasūtra
cite.paraphrase: Dhyāna is of four kinds: ārta (pained), raudra (fierce), dharmya (of dharma) and śukla (white).

statement: Each names a mind that will not stay. Gītā: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (BhG 6.34). Vyāsa: samādhi is a property of the mind at every level, and one of its grounds is the distracted (vikṣipta) (YB 1.1). cite.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
cite.original: 4. Dhammānupassanā 4.1. Dhammānupassanānīvaraṇapabba Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa kāmacchandassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa kāmacchandassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa byāpādassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa byāpādassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa byāpādassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa thinamiddhassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa thinamiddhassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa uddhaccakukkuccassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. cite.paraphrase: Contemplation of dhammas, first section: the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating dhammas in dhammas with regard to the five hindrances. Here, when sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is present in him he knows 'there is sensual desire in me'; when it is absent he knows 'there is no sensual desire in me'; he knows how unarisen sensual desire comes to arise; he knows how arisen sensual desire is abandoned; and he knows how the abandoned sensual desire will not arise again in the future. He does the same, in exactly this fivefold way, for ill will (byāpāda), for dullness and drowsiness (thina-middha), for restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) and for doubt (vicikicchā).

It is not a finding about any person, and it makes no health claim.

cite.paraphrase: Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is that by which one sees wrongly, or which sees wrongly, or mere wrong seeing: its mark is unwise insistence; its function is clinging; its manifestation is wrong adherence; its proximate cause is the wish not to see the noble ones and the like; it is to be regarded as the most blameworthy. Restlessness (uddhacca) is agitated state: its mark is non-calming; its function is unsteadiness, like water stirred by wind; its manifestation is bewilderment, like a flag fluttering in the wind or like ashes thrown up by a blow on a stone; its proximate cause is unwise attention to the non-calming of the mind; it is to be regarded as distraction of consciousness. The other factors are as stated for the unwholesome. The second unwholesome consciousness is like the first, but prompted and with sloth-torpor indeterminate. Sloth (thīna) is the sinking, torpor (middha) the drowsing: sloth has as its mark lack of energy and as function dispelling energy, as manifestation sinking; torpor has as mark unworkableness, as function smothering, as manifestation drooping or drowsy sleep; for both the proximate cause is unwise attention to discontent, lazy stretching and the like. Conceit (māna), indeterminate in the third and fourth, has as mark haughtiness, as function self-promotion, as manifestation vain-glory, as proximate cause greed dissociated from view; it is to be regarded as madness. The fifth to eighth are given in the same manner without wrong view or with joy left out.

statement: You wrote "At night my mind runs like a sewing machine"; the texts describe this as the mind moving off wherever it will, restless and unsteady (bhg 6.26, 6.34).

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original:
yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram|
tatastato niyamyaitadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: wherever the restless (cañcala), unsteady mind wanders off, from there he should restrain it and bring it back under control in the self alone.

statement: Your words “At night my mind runs like a sewing machine” may fit what the Vedic and yogic texts call Cañcala manas (the restless mind). Arjuna: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate; I think it as hard to hold as the wind (BhG 6.34). Kṛṣṇa: no doubt the mind is hard to hold and moving, but it is held by practice and dispassion (6.35). The turbulent senses carry off by force the mind even of a wise man who strives (2.60); the mind that follows the roving senses carries off understanding as the wind a ship on the water (2.67).

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original:
indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano'nuvidhīyate|
tadasya harati prajñāṃ vāyurnāvamivāmbhasi
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: for when the mind (manas) is led along by the roving senses, it carries off his wisdom (prajñā), as the wind carries off a ship on the water.
